raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that electric cars generally cost the least amount of money per month while also creating the least average carbon emissions per mile. Additionally, traditional gas powered cars create the most amount of carbon emissions per mile, but can range in price from most expensive to least expensive per month. This is likely because traditional gas-powered cars are the most abundantly distributed car. Hybrid cars are an average of traditional gas-powered cars and electric cars. They emit less carbon dioxide per mile than gas-powered cars, but the emit more carbon dioxide per mile than electric cars. 

What do you wonder?
From what I have heard from my peers, people refrain from thinking about buying electric cars because they believe they are too expensive. If people knew about the cost efficiency of electric cars, would they be more willing to buy them? 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
The current climate crisis will ultimately effect almost every person in my generation. Many scientists believe that air pollution has caused an increase in cancers, cognitive decline, and depression. Carbon emissions are one of the most significant causes of this air pollution. Thus, the information in this graph should be used to motivate people to buy electric cars instead of traditional gas-powered cars.

raw_comment: Based on the data presented in the graph, our group found that there are five main groups of vehicles presented, consisting of traditional gas-powered cars, diesel cars, hybrid vehicles, fuel cell, and electric cars. The dots, representing a specific car make, all have a wide range in average cost per month and CO2 emissions per mile. Furthermore, we noticed gas-powered cars have the highest emissions rate while also maintaining a high average cost. Electric cars, on the other hand, had mostly similar monthly costs as their gas-powered counterparts but had far fewer emissions per mile. Based on these observations, we wondered what if the size of a car had any correlation to CO2 emission levels as well as if the dots that are clustered together have the same manufacturer? Lastly, our group analyzed the impact that the data presented in this graph had on us and our community. In today’s environment where pollution is a major topic, this graph helped reveal what cars are not only environmentally friendly, but also helped save consumer’s money. Our headline for this graph would be, “Average Cost per Month vs. Average CO2 Emissions for Different Fuel Using Cars.”

raw_comment:
My team noticed that gas cars are more expensive than electric cars (which was contrary to what most of us had naturally assumed). We also noticed that there’s an outlying piece of data with the intriguing name of a fuel cell car. 
After looking upon this beautiful graph, my team and I had a few questions pop into our minds, such as: Do you think the number of fuel cars will increase in coming years? And if so, by how much? Why are there so few fuel cell cars? Are they really expensive to make? Why do gas cars have such a wide range of CO2 emissions?
We also had a few questions on how this might impact our community: Will charging stations be popping up around the community for the convenience of electric car owners? Will electric cars become more common?
As a final task, our group was asked to create a catchy headline that could capture the attention of such a grand audience as those who read The New York Times. Personally, I love to be dramatic, and as the scribe of our group I have full reign over adding whatever amount of soap opera I want to the headline, so in the end, our two possible titles turned out to be something like this:  “The Cost of Humanities Future” and “Carbon Boom or Bust”

Title: How to save your money and the environment 
From the average carbon dioxide emissions per mile graph we noticed lots of interesting information. First, we noticed that traditional gas owned cars have the widest range in carbon dioxide emissions. At the top of this range, the Toyota Sequoia emits above 800 grams of co2 per mile. At the lower end of this range, the honda civic emits around 300 grams of co2. Second, we noticed the more carbon dioxide emitted from the vehicle, the more the average cost monthly to maintain the vehicle with the expectation being the fuel cell car. 
Finally, we noticed that electric cars have the least amount of carbon emission per mile which makes sense and then the hybrid cars are a little above the electric. I wonder why some cars are way more costly than others. I also wonder how a hybrid car could be just as spendy as a diesel car. Another thing I wonder is how a hybrid car could cost just as much as a regular gas car. This impacts us and our communities by showing us what cars pollute the most and which are the most eco friendly, such as the Toyota Sequoia which produces almost 800 grams of carbon emissions every single mile! Compared to something much much more eco friendly like a Honda Ionic which doesn't even hit 200 grams per mile.

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?” shows the benefits to the environment in terms of the budget costs for nearly every new model of cars, SUVs and other models that sell for $55,000 or less.  The graph appeared in The New York Times.  Which cars reduce the true costs of our car-buying decisions – both for the planet and our budgets?

From 9 am – 2 pm ET today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  Plus, please share a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” website, the link to the article that included this graph and much more.  

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs). 
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and

Keep noticing and wondering.  Next week’s graph will be posted by Friday.    The topic – professional sports players and coaches.
